raw_response:
Alright, let me think about this year's plan for my 1.5 mu.

My wheat's already in the ground since last October — I put in 济麦22 (Jimai 22), seed I saved from last year's harvest so that's no cash out. Before planting I had the tractor man come rotary-till and I broadcast about 45 kg of compound fertilizer (15-15-15, 复合肥) per mu as base. That's what the agricultural station has been telling us for years and it's what works. Now it's April, the wheat is jointing. Back in early March when it was greening up I already did the first irrigation and topdressed about 20 kg of urea per mu. The wheat looks alright — color is good, tillers are decent. I'll water it again at heading in early May, and probably once more at grain filling if the rains don't come. In this area with well irrigation it's not too expensive but it's not free — the pump uses electricity and we pay by the hour.

For pesticide on wheat: I did the herbicide spray back in March for broadleaf weeds. I'll keep an eye out for powdery mildew — my neighbor老张's field had it bad last year, so if I see the white patches I'll spray fungicide once. I'm expecting maybe 430 kg/mu off the wheat, similar to last year.

Then as soon as wheat is off in early June, I turn right around and plant maize the same week — no time to plow, I just pay for the no-till planter to come through with Zhengdan 958 (郑单958) seed, about 3-4 kg per mu. Put down another 30 kg compound with planting. Then at big bell stage (大喇叭口期) end of July I'll topdress 20 kg urea per mu. Maize doesn't need much irrigation here — the summer rains usually handle it — but if it's really dry in July I'll pump once or twice. Herbicide goes down right after planting before emergence. Corn borer shows up in July so I'll spray once. Expecting around 480 kg/mu.

The whole farm is just 1.5 mu so we don't hire anyone — me and my wife do everything except the machinery work (tractor, planter, combine all hired from the village service). My older son and his wife work in Handan, younger boy is in school, so it's just the two of us in the field. Most of this grain we keep for ourselves — we eat our own flour and grind our own maize meal. The extra maize we sell to pay back the fertilizer bill. Off-farm money is what really supports the family; the land is mostly for food security and so the land doesn't go idle.
